title: Having Chubby Jackson and Oscar Pettiford as two basses
summary: Barnet hired Oscar Pettiford in Minneapolis in 1943 to join Chubby Jackson, but the two bassists could not get along and Pettiford left.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Well, that -- well, first of all, about, "Jam Session," that was recorded all over the -- filmed all over the country, and then they sewed it together in Hollywood,

so I can imagine how disjointed -- I never saw it, but I can imagine how -- what a cross patched, messed up thing it must be. Some of it was done in New York, some was done in Hollywood, and then, you know, they just recorded and filmed segments and sewed it together afterwards. They wrote the story afterwards, I think, and fit in all these things. If there was a story. Oh, you asked about Pettiford. Well, we were playing -- in 1943, we were playing the Orpheum Theater in Minneapolis, and Chubby came in and he said, "Hey, I've got a bass player, heard a bass player last night, you've got to hear him." So I said, "Where does he play?" He said, "He's downstairs. I've got him here." So Oscar -- it was Oscar Pettiford, you know, and Oscar went right ahead and played me a whole bass fiddle concerto, all by himself, and I said, "What are you doing? Are you working?" And he said, "No, just a few jobs around." And I said, "How would you like to come with the band." I said, "We'll have two basses." He said, "Oh, I'd love that." And Chubby was delighted, you know. And we started out and everything was fine. Then, after oh, two, three, four months went by, I had them doing things together, I had a concerto written for the both of them which involved comedy, dancing and playing and everything. It was a cute thing. We did it at the Capitol Theater in New York and people who saw it said it was one of the most entertaining band things, that particular thing, you know, that they'd

ever seen, but now Chubby comes to me and he says, "Charlie, Oscar ain't making it." I said, "Oh, really?" He said, "No, no, he's not making it." The next day Oscar comes to me and he says, "Charlie, I hate to say this but Chubby ain't making it." And they finally wound up, with Oscar said he couldn't stand it any longer, and I had a contract with Chubby. I said, "There isn't anything I can do, I've got to honor the contract, and if you're unhappy, which I'm very sorry," -- Oscar -- I don't know where he went, but Oscar and I were very close friends. I mean we used to go out together in New York and make all the joints, and he was a wonderful guy and certainly a very talented bass player.
Yeah. Yeah. Had he -- I know Minneapolis is his home. Had he travelled before that?

I don't think to any extent. He might have gone, you know, on a gig someplace for a couple of days with some band or something, but no, he was just jobbing around Minneapolis. The whole family was there. He has a sister and --
They had a family band originally, I know.
Yeah. It was a very musical family.
What a shame that Chubby and Oscar couldn't get along. That must have been -- did you ever record with both basses?
